title: English Tenses – B1
description: This B1 course reviews the main English tenses: present simple and continuous, present perfect, past simple and the future with will and going to.

lessons.title: Present simple vs present continuous
lessons.description: Habits and general truths versus actions happening now.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to the first lesson of this course on English tenses.
We use the present simple for habits, routines and general truths.
For example: I drink coffee every morning, and water boils at one hundred degrees.
With he, she and it we add an s to the verb: she works, he plays.
The present continuous describes an action happening now, at the moment of speaking.
It is formed with am, is or are plus the verb ending in ing: I am reading.
Stative verbs like know, like and want are not normally used in the continuous form.

lessons.title: Present perfect
lessons.description: Form and uses of the present perfect, for and since, ever and never.

segments.text: In this lesson we study the present perfect.
The present perfect is formed with have or has plus the past participle.
We use it for life experiences without a specific time: I have visited Japan twice.
With for and since we talk about a duration that continues until now.
For is followed by a period of time, like for ten years; since is followed by a starting point, like since 2019.
Ever and never are common in questions and negatives: Have you ever eaten sushi? I have never seen snow.

lessons.title: Past simple
lessons.description: Finished actions in the past, regular and irregular verbs.

segments.text: Now let us look at the past simple.
We use the past simple for finished actions at a specific time in the past, like yesterday or last week.
Regular verbs take ed: worked, played, visited.
Many common verbs are irregular, for example go becomes went and see becomes saw.
A common mistake is to use the present perfect with a finished time expression: say I saw him yesterday, not I have seen him yesterday.
This lesson is about talking about the future.
We use will for decisions made at the moment of speaking and for predictions without evidence.
We use going to for plans and intentions decided before speaking: I am going to study medicine.
Going to is also used for predictions based on present evidence: look at those clouds, it is going to rain.
